performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
intro: Hartmann’s gate was never built in Kyiv; Mussorgsky’s final movement sets it in E♭ major. The movement includes brass, a chant and pealing bells.

sections.label: A · Brass gate theme in E♭ major
sections.mNote: Broad chords, marked majestic and grand.

sections.label: B · A chant in A♭ minor
sections.mNote: Plain chordal phrases replace the broad brass tune.

sections.label: A′ · Gate theme over running scales
sections.mNote: The E♭ major theme returns over running octave scales.

sections.label: B′ · The chant in E♭ minor
sections.mNote: The hymn returns a fifth higher.

sections.label: C · Bell figures and Promenade theme
sections.mNote: Low repeated notes build into overlapping bell figures.

sections.label: A″ · Gate theme, meno mosso
sections.mNote: Meno mosso; the melody broadens above three-part beats.

sections.label: D · Repeated chords above a moving bass
sections.mNote: The bass moves beneath repeated triplet chords.

sections.label: A‴ · Final statement in E♭
sections.mNote: Broad chords and bell figures close the suite.

cues.title: Opening theme in E♭ major, brass
cues.text: The brass open in E♭ major with the main theme. Mussorgsky’s directions are Maestoso and Con grandezza, majestic and with grandeur. Broad chords support the melody, and softer woodwinds reply between its phrases.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, opening bars; orchestration: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, 7 April 2022, p. 7: https://philharmonia-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/2022/04/07.04.22_RFH-online.pdf. Ravel attribution for this recording remains inferred.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hartmann’s design for the Kyiv gate
cues.text: Hartmann’s design has tinted brick, an imperial eagle and a three-storey belfry with a cupola shaped like a Slavic helmet. The planned stone gates of Kyiv were never built. Mussorgsky’s movement includes writing for bells.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg describes the unbuilt design and its belfry: https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition. The bell writing is discussed by Orrin Howard: https://www.laphil.com/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition-modest-mussorgsky-zs2phpn9

cues.title: Dedication to Stasov, 1874
cues.text: Mussorgsky finished the suite on 22 June 1874. Five days later he inscribed the title page with a tribute to Vladimir Stasov, and a month after that he added a note that he meant to publish it. The suite appeared only in 1886, five years after his death, in Rimsky-Korsakov’s edition.
cues.evidence: Mussorgsky’s autograph (Russian National Library; scan at IMSLP #733281): the last page is signed in Saint Petersburg on 22 June 1874; the title page is headed “Dedicated to Vladimir Vasilyevich Stasov”, carries an inscription to Stasov dated 27 June, and a note “for printing” dated 26 July. Published in 1886 by Bessel in Rimsky-Korsakov’s edition (IMSLP #85544). Completion by 22 June: Michael Steinberg, https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition

cues.title: Return of the gate theme, E♭ major
cues.text: The gate theme returns in E♭ major, played by the brass. Strings and woodwinds play rising and falling scales around the brass melody.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 47–63; strings and wind runs around the brass melody: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, p. 7.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ravel’s orchestration, Paris, 1922
cues.text: In the summer of 1922 Ravel orchestrated Mussorgsky’s piano suite for Serge Koussevitzky. Koussevitzky conducted the first performance in Paris on 22 October. In 1930 he recorded it with the Boston Symphony Orchestra.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg gives the commission, 22 October 1922 Paris première and 1930 Boston recording: https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition

cues.title: Return of the Promenade
cues.text: The Promenade theme returns within the bell passage (bars 97–110 in Lamm’s piano edition). In the orchestral version it was first played by a single trumpet. Quick figures above and below it continue the bell pattern.
cues.evidence: Peter Laki identifies the late Promenade return: https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition-mussorgsky. Lamm’s piano edition, bars 97–110, places it within the bell passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Main theme at Meno mosso
cues.text: The main theme broadens at Meno mosso, sempre maestoso (slower, still majestic). Its chords sound against minim triplets. The bass and upper parts alternate across several octaves.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 114–135, Meno mosso and minim triplets: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/MussorgskyM/pictures-at-an-exhibition/pictures-at-an-exhibition-lys/great-gate-meno.ily
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rising bass under repeated chords
cues.text: Repeated chords continue in minim triplets while the bass rises from A♭ to B♭ and C♭. The triplet pulse holds through each change of harmony, and a crescendo begins.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 136–155: minim triplets, A♭–B♭–C♭ bass and crescendo; Mutopia transcription.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final chords in E♭
cues.text: The last statement broadens further, marked Grave, sempre allargando. Low E♭ sustains the full chords, and the closing pages span the whole range of the orchestra. The suite ends on E♭.
cues.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 162–173, Grave, sempre allargando and final E♭ octaves; Mutopia transcription. Ravel’s full orchestral ending is described in Joanna Wyld’s Philharmonia guide.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: E♭ major statement to A♭ minor chant
transitions.from: A · Brass gate theme in E♭ major
transitions.to: B · A chant in A♭ minor
transitions.how: The broad E♭ major statement ends, and an A♭ minor chord begins the chant (bars 29–46 in Lamm’s piano edition). The score marks it senza espressione, without expression, and the notes move together in plain chords. In Ravel’s orchestration the brass-led tune is followed by quieter woodwinds.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 29–46: A♭ minor chant and senza espressione; woodwind contrast: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, p. 7.

transitions.title: E♭ major returns with running octaves
transitions.from: B · A chant in A♭ minor
transitions.to: A′ · Gate theme over running scales
transitions.how: The chant ends on the bare fifth A♭–E♭. E♭ major returns under a descending scale marked energico. In the orchestration, Ravel keeps the main tune in the brass while the strings and woodwinds play fast running figures around it.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 45–55; orchestration: Joanna Wyld, Philharmonia listening guide, p. 7.

transitions.title: The chant returns a fifth higher
transitions.from: A′ · Gate theme over running scales
transitions.to: B′ · The chant in E♭ minor
transitions.how: The running octaves climb to B♭ and stop. The chant then begins again in E♭ minor, a fifth above its first appearance. It keeps its long notes and the marking senza espressione, with G♭ in place of the G♮ of the gate theme.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 63–80: ascent to B♭ and E♭ minor transposition of the chant, marked senza espressione; Mutopia transcription.

transitions.title: Low bell figures overlap
transitions.from: B′ · The chant in E♭ minor
transitions.to: C · Bell figures and Promenade theme
transitions.how: The hymn ends on a bare fifth, E♭ and B♭. Low A♭ and C♭ then alternate in the bass beneath repeated upper notes. Triplets enter, then quavers, and the bell figures overlap more closely as the note values shorten before the Promenade theme returns.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 79–97: bare fifth, alternating A♭/C♭ bass and progressively shorter note values. Orrin Howard’s LA Phil note describes the bells.

transitions.title: Scale to low C; gate theme returns
transitions.from: C · Bell figures and Promenade theme
transitions.how: A descending scale runs to low C and stops under a fermata. At Meno mosso, sempre maestoso the gate theme returns in E♭ major. Its first chord has G in the bass, and broad triplets now carry the melody across the orchestra.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 111–120: descending scale to C, fermata and Meno mosso return over G; Mutopia transcription.

transitions.title: A♭ bass under F minor seventh
transitions.to: D · Repeated chords above a moving bass
transitions.how: The gate theme closes on E♭. The bass then moves to A♭ beneath an F minor seventh chord (F–A♭–C–E♭), which is repeated in broad triplets. B♭ and C♭ follow in the bass while the chords continue to sound, and a crescendo begins.
transitions.evidence: Lamm’s piano edition, bars 134–155: E♭ close, F–A♭–C–E♭ chord over A♭, moving bass and crescendo; Mutopia transcription.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive; conductor unknown)
fields.note: The Commons page names no performer (“see Musopen for performance author information”). The Free Music Archive album of 15 tracks by the Skidmore College Orchestra lists a track of the same title and length (5:29; this file is 5:28), and the Internet Archive item for the first Promenade credits the same orchestra. The identification of this file with that track rests on title and length; the Musopen performer page was not opened. Conductor: unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: No session date is documented. The Internet Archive item says “date unknown, 2008 at the latest”; the Free Music Archive lists the album as released 6 April 2009; this file was uploaded to Commons on 2008-01-21. None of these is a recording date.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 1 — recording release: PD-author public-domain dedication by Musopen, with Wikimedia VRTS permission ticket 2008012110017088.
fields.note: The file description applies PD-author|Musopen to the recording separately from PD-old-100 for the music, and cites the VRTS ticket; the page is in “Items with VRTS permission confirmed”. Musopen’s reproduced policy says the music is public domain with no restrictions; its requests not to sell the recordings and to credit Musopen are courtesy requests, not a non-commercial licence. The Internet Archive copy of the first Promenade is marked CC0 1.0. Session date is not needed for this route.

composer.epithet: Composer who could make a singer sound like a frightened child, a drunken monk or a tsar who could no longer bear his own thoughts.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition with Mily Balakirev, outside the conservatory
Guards officer until 1858; later a clerk in the Forestry Department and Government Control
Borodin, Cui, Balakirev, Rimsky-Korsakov; Vladimir Stasov and Viktor Hartmann
Boris Godunov, unfinished operas, three song cycles, Pictures at an Exhibition
composer.background:
When Borodin met Mussorgsky at a Saint Petersburg military hospital in 1856, the seventeen-year-old officer was immaculate, with a close-fitting uniform, polished manners and well-kept hands. He played extracts from Il trovatore and La traviata at the piano while admirers gathered round. Twenty-five years later, in another hospital, Repin painted the portrait that became his most familiar likeness. It shows a man in a dressing gown, his hair in disorder and his eyes still alert.

Mussorgsky was born at Karevo, on his family’s estate. His mother taught him the piano, and his nurse’s stories prompted the improvisations he remembered from childhood. At ten he was sent to school in Saint Petersburg, where he studied piano with Anton Gerke. He entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852 and received a commission in the Preobrazhensky Regiment in 1856. His father paid for the publication of his first piano piece, a polka.
